#6063. American Airlines Reverses Its Original New York Strategy—Wants Local Customers Back In Major Cities

American Airlines says focusing on local customers has produced “material margin improvement” at LaGuardia. They’re doing better in New York by focusing on the needs of New Yorkers. Meanwhile, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said at at Thursday’s Skift Aviation Forum that he sees Chicago’s biggest opportunity in winning corporate traffic, and he’s working on Los Angeles schedules that better serve the people who live there too. That’s a full rejection of the New York strategy American laid out in 2014, immediately after the US Airways merger. They wanted to bring passengers to New York, rather than offer a schedule for New Yorkers. That was dumb. They thought they couldn’t compete in New York, and they walked away from the credit card spending of New Yorkers. American Chose Not To Be The Airline For New Yorkers The original post-merger strategy was building schedules around people coming to New York for business and then going home. Arriving in the morning and leaving in the evening works for an out of town visitor. A New Yorker making a day trip wants the reverse. American dropped LaGuardia service to Cleveland, Minneapolis and Atlanta while adding cities like Roanoke and Wilmington, North Carolina. They were using scarce New York slots to strengthen their appeal to customers they believed were underserved elsewhere in the country, instead of building a schedule to take people who lived in New York to the places they needed to go. It was an extension of the old US Airways playbook of avoiding direct competition. By 2018, Robert Isom was pitching a boutique business airline for New York, built around London, premium transcons and a limited collection of other routes. That was already a change from the original inbound strategy. It still missed that the person buying a business class ticket to London also takes their family on vacation. And by not providing either a better product or a more well-rounded schedule, they were setting themselves up to be a ‘spill carrier’ taking business only when offering a lower price that competitors wouldn’t meet. The JetBlue partnership demonstrated what a broader network could do. In October 2021, I reported American’s fastest growing markets for AAdvantage signups were its JetBlue and Alaska partnership cities. Doug Parker Explained The Credit Card Math Problem In March, I wrote about former American CEO Doug Parker’s explanation of how airlines allocate credit card revenue to routes. He described assigning the money to flights where customers redeem their miles. That accounts for the seats being used. It doesn’t tell you which flights caused the customer to get the card and put spending on it in the first place. A New Yorker might use their miles for Hawaii. But they chose American because it worked for their trips to Chicago, London and Miami. If American stops being useful for those trips, the customer may switch airlines and cards. Crediting the Hawaii flight doesn’t capture what the New York schedule was doing for the business. That was my criticism of American’s retreat seven and eight years ago: cutting a flight can improve its route accounting while making the company worse off by losing the customer’s other business. You can’t count the card revenue twice, but you need to count what disappears when the customer leaves. Chicago And Los Angeles Need The Same Rethink This is also why the O’Hare fight matters beyond departure counts and Scott Kirby’s desire to beat American. At the employee meeting I covered in January, Pieper reported 20% growth in Chicago loyalty enrollments and 20% growth in card acquisitions over the preceding nine months. As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May said their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects. Meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s plans to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier: I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the big markets in the world In his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the plan was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30. American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation. American has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens. So 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will! The Alaska Partnership Fits This, Too American nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results. In October 2021, I reported American’s fastest growing markets for AAdvantage signups were its JetBlue and Alaska partnership cities. Doug Parker Explained The Credit Card Math Problem In March, I wrote about former American CEO Doug Parker’s explanation of how airlines allocate credit card revenue to routes. He described assigning the money to flights where customers redeem their miles. That accounts for the seats being used. It doesn’t tell you which flights caused the customer to get the card and put spending on it in the first place. A New Yorker might use their miles for Hawaii. But they chose American because it worked for their trips to Chicago, London and Miami. If American stops being useful for those trips, the customer may switch airlines and cards. Crediting the Hawaii flight doesn’t capture what the New York schedule was doing for the business. That was my criticism of American’s retreat seven and eight years ago: cutting a flight can improve its route accounting while making the company worse off by losing the customer’s other business. You can’t count the card revenue twice, but you need to count what disappears when the customer leaves. Chicago And Los Angeles Need The Same Rethink This is also why the O’Hare fight matters beyond departure counts and Scott Kirby’s desire to beat American. At the employee meeting I covered in January, Pieper reported 20% growth in Chicago loyalty enrollments and 20% growth in card acquisitions over the preceding nine months. As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May said their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects. Meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s plans to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier: I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the big markets in the world In his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the plan was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30. American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation. American has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens. So 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will! The Alaska Partnership Fits This, Too American nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results. The original post-merger strategy was building schedules around people coming to New York for business and then going home. Arriving in the morning and leaving in the evening works for an out of town visitor. A New Yorker making a day trip wants the reverse.

American dropped LaGuardia service to Cleveland, Minneapolis and Atlanta while adding cities like Roanoke and Wilmington, North Carolina. They were using scarce New York slots to strengthen their appeal to customers they believed were underserved elsewhere in the country, instead of building a schedule to take people who lived in New York to the places they needed to go. It was an extension of the old US Airways playbook of avoiding direct competition.

By 2018, Robert Isom was pitching a boutique business airline for New York, built around London, premium transcons and a limited collection of other routes. That was already a change from the original inbound strategy. It still missed that the person buying a business class ticket to London also takes their family on vacation. And by not providing either a better product or a more well-rounded schedule, they were setting themselves up to be a ‘spill carrier’ taking business only when offering a lower price that competitors wouldn’t meet.

I’m not surprised to hear AA talking about wanting to be more competitive in New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles. They’ve been running a promo, seemingly targeted at travelers who have flown American for business, offering bonus miles for segments to/from/through NYC/ORD/LAX.

AA is finally starting to learn the lesson that George Costanza learned. Every instinct that they have had for the past 10 years has been wrong. So, just do the opposite.

You really do have to wonder how much longer Devon May can survive. He’s been on the wrong side of every product decision at AA and been the key voice against product improvement.

But it’s also a very AA phenomenon — keeping bad leaders who have never shown a shred of strategic thinking.

Speaking from the position of a +40 year ~4 million-mile Platinum Pro A/Advantage customer, when American began abandoning New York for both transcontinental and international flights, I began abandoning American and it will take a lot to bring me and many other top tier former loyal NYC area customers back. Unfortunately, the airline has been mismanaged and mistreated loyal customers since Bob Crandell left in 1998 and both shareholders and loyal customers have suffered. It’s time for a major overall of both senior management and the Board and a new attitude/approach from American’s current poor customer service team.

Day by day Nat and Heather are fixing the Vasu, Parker and Isom effups.

They can reshuffle the existing fleet to serve both segments…early morning locals departing the hub and early morning visitors to the hub.

This is good to see and it is reflected in the schedules (for example, JFK-ORD is now 4 x daily) and the resumption of JFK-SEA with 2 x daily (which will be complemented by the AS flying). AA has some holes to fill in its NY portfolio. It should fly from JFK to SAT for example, and continue to pick up markets that B6 is walking away from. Eventually, American will have the majority of the B6 portfolio to themselves and that will unlock their ability to be a competitive force in the NYC market. AA must still continue to refine and improve its offering and maintain and grow the pivot to premium. The money is in the NYC, Chicago, and LA markets, not in the sunbelt.

@Gary–This article is an excellent analysis. I agree that flight times are important to local passengers. When I visit NYC or Chicago, I like to depart such that I arrive in the mid to late afternoon. That allows me to check into a hotel upon arrival and have the evening to get a good meal, go to a show, erc. I like to come home on a late afternoon flight ti maximize my time on the trip. (That kind of scheduling appeals to leisure travelers as well as business travelers.). If I lived in NY or Chicago, I would like similar schedules if flying west.

@Joe–I agree that whenever possible, an airline should try to schedule in a way that works for both ends of the city pair.

@Peter – exactly right! Best post of the day.

I would add AA needs to add back a few non stop flights from NY and BOS to South Florida and Orlando. This is the key to winning the NY/ BOS domestic market.

Seems like Parker and Kerr (the US Airways CFO who served at AA until 2023, promoting May) were the ones who are most responsible for where we are now – finance ran the show. Vasu, and even Isom inherited a lot of the implications of their thinking.

And let’s not forget Kirby before he learned new ways at United – decisions in the early 2010s set up the fleet and network we have today

Southwest has a miniscule presence in New York. Delta has a miniscule presence in Chicago. Yet both are much more profitable than American. How can that be?

@DesertGhost – Delta has #1 at JFK/LGA and #1 at LAX. They themselves say the reason for AUS expansion is card revenue. Southwest is huge in California. Huge in Florida. And has lower costs. And their profits aren’t that much higher than American’s.

AA should also try to add SAN, maybe CPH and ZRH from JFK. Also should build more of a focus city at Boston Logan. There is card revenue there!

Is it possible AA could get from ~11% of JFK market share to 15-20%?

this is precisely why Scott Kirby is paranoid.

AA is coming back and UA can no longer count on revenue that AA has been bleeding for years.

DL’s focus on “stealing from” AA was largely pre-covid and at LAX during covid. DL is comfortable w/ its domestic size now and is not focused on market share and is reaping the profits accordingly even while continuing to take share from B6 in the NE.

AA is the largest domestic airline because of their size in a whole lot of small and medium sized cities.

AA steal carries a lot of low fare traffic it should not be carrying but it cannot get rid of it until it replaces it with higher quality revenue in coastal cities.

Gary – you did the math wrong on LAX gates. American has five “permanent” priority use gates at TBIT and five temporary gates due to T5 construction. When construction ends it will still have those five gates. That’s where the 30 comes from. But what AA ultimately wants is 35.

The situation with the five TBIT gates it permanently holds is that it has priority first use of four of them, and the fifth is triggered by minimum usage of the first four. It also does need to share these with BA, QF and JAL.

Two words describe why this 3M miler Southern Californian no longer flies AA out of LAX,for work or vacation. “Eagles Nest”.

The place is a dump, the crowded buses are insufferable, and T4 is a construction nightmare. UA was smart dumping that remote terminal many years ago.

How the hell does Isom still have a job? How the hell does Dougie sleep at night?

#6062. Copa 737 & UPS 767 Collide On Miami Airport Taxiway: Pilot Blames Checklist Distraction

Last night, a Copa Boeing 737 and a UPS Boeing 767 collided on a taxiway at Miami International Airport (MIA). South Florida is known for its horrendous drivers, and I guess that trend is making its way to the taxiways at airports as well.

This accident happened shortly after 9PM on Saturday, November 14, 2026. It involves a Copa Boeing 737-800 that had just arrived from Panama City (PTY) as flight CM427, and a UPS Boeing 767-300 that was getting ready to depart to Bogota (BOG) as flight 5X358.

The UPS 767 had been advised to give way to the Copa 737 on the taxiway, but the pilots failed to do that. As a result, the wing of the Copa 737 hit the nose of the UPS 767. While a full investigation will of course be performed, the air traffic control audio gives us a good sense of what happened:

Copa pilot: “427, somebody hit us.”ATC: “427, roger. UPS, you’re supposed to give way to the 73 there.”UPS pilot: “Roger, we running checklist, runway change.”ATC: “UPS 358, did you hit that aircraft?”UPS pilot: “Yeah, we went too far, and then he clipped us with the wing.”

So as you can see, the UPS pilots were at fault here, and the excuse seems to be that they were distracted because they were going through checklists because of a runway change.

Fortunately there were no major injuries, but two people on the Copa flight did complain of minor back pain. The damage to the planes is extensive, though, including to the nose of the UPS 767 and the left wing of the Copa 737.

Taxiway contact at MIA last night.Copa 737 left wingtip into the nose of a UPS 767. UPS was instructed to give way, crew acknowledged they went too far. Two treated for minor injuries on scene. pic.twitter.com/sB0kJamQ3J

That UPS B767 looks pissed after clipping the winglet of that Copa Airlines B737! https://t.co/9vu34jsVkk pic.twitter.com/e0l5ergWei

Can I just respectfully make a point here, without being sarcastic? If the accident were reversed here, and the female, foreign pilot had been at fault for this, we would immediately see people screaming “DEI.” Meanwhile when someone sounds like your average American dude, we just consider it to be an honest mistake.

The concept of “DEI” in the aviation world is not about hiring unqualified people, but it’s about expanding the potential pool of people who could qualify for a job, so that the best people can be hired.

Why do I even bring this up now? Well, remember the recent Amazon Air crash at Miami Airport? When the air traffic control audio came out, people heard a foreign accent from the pilot. People immediately started yelling “DEI,” talking about H1-B visas, etc.

However, that was the pilot communicating, and the pilot actually flying was a white, older, ex-military dude. And he was flying completely recklessly, and failed to listen to the first officer’s warnings. I know it’s hard when reality doesn’t match people’s narratives, but that’s why I feel like it’s important to call these things out.

A major corporation, Amazon, subcontracts with other foreign carriers to operate their aircraft. What I’m saying is a few of those subcontractors hire lesser qualified crews and maintenance, resulting in what happened in Miami. And, I’m sure DEI plays a role. In my estimation,… https://t.co/GhFeJHMuMK

Presumably this is coincidental, but I think it’s interesting to note that on November 5, 2026, there was a very close call on a taxiway at Miami Airport, not that far from where this happened.

A Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 was departing to Frankfurt (FRA) as LH463, and an American Boeing 787-8 had just arrived from Philadelphia (PHL) as AA1155. The American 787 was advised to “give way to Lufthansa off the right,” which… they then failed to do.

As you’d expect, the Lufthansa pilots took the situation very seriously. The Lufthansa pilot said “we had to make a full stop at a full taxi speed, American is turning in our way.” The air traffic controller responded by saying “they’ve made every wrong turn possible” (in reference to the American plane — which I don’t actually think is true here). The Lufthansa pilot said they’d file a report, because that “was very close to an accident in the making.”

I love how German the Lufthansa pilot is in how he handles this, and how he finishes by saying “you need to make sure stuff like that doesn’t happen too often.” Lol, you don’t say…

A Copa Boeing 737 and a UPS Boeing 767 had an accident on a taxiway at Miami Airport. The UPS 767 was supposed to give way to the Copa 737, but failed to do so, as the pilots claimed they were distracted by their checklists.

This accident took out a chunk of the wing of the Copa 737, and did quite a bit of damage to the nose of the UPS 767 as well. Earlier this month, a very close call between a Lufthansa 747 and American 787 also got quite a bit of attention, but fortunately this had a better outcome.

What do you make of this Miami Airport accident?

#6061. United Raises Credit Card Bonuses To 100,000 Miles—Cardholders Earn More On Flights And Pay Less For Awards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

United and Chase have raised initial bonuses on all four personal credit cards, with offers now reaching 100,000 miles. That’s worth considering because United has made its credit card much harder to skip: eligible primary cardholders earn more miles for flying, then pay fewer miles to book United awards. Even elite status doesn’t eliminate the disadvantage of going without one.

I’ve written about United cutting mileage-earning for customers without a card while giving cardholders more. If you’re active with the airline and MileagePlus, you need to look at the cost of a card against the miles you’re giving up without it. And with the annual fee cards, you don’t have to put all your spending on one to get the better flight earning and award pricing.

Here’s the current lineup. Each offer has a spending component plus another 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user (an employee card on the business products) within three months of account opening. Card    Initial Bonus    Purchases In First 3 Months    Annual Fee United GatewaySM Card (See rates and fees) 40,000 after $1,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user50,000 total $1,000 $0 UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) 70,000 after $3,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user80,000 total $3,000 $0 first year, then $150 United QuestSM Card (See rates and fees) 80,000 after $4,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user90,000 total $4,000 $350 United ClubSM Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $695 UnitedSM Business Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $150 There are also elite status incentives: Quest: 500 Premier qualifying points after your first purchase. Business: 2,000 Premier qualifying points after the same $5,000 in purchases within three months that earns the mileage bonus. The extra 10,000 miles for adding a user are awarded once per account, and that user must remain on the account when the bonus is fulfilled. What You’re Giving Up Without A Qualifying Card For United tickets purchased on or after April 2, 2026, here’s what the airline awards for flying. The cardholder column applies to the primary holder of an eligible annual fee card. The United GatewaySM Card requires spending to qualify. MileagePlus Status    Without A Qualifying Card    With A Qualifying Card General member 3 miles per dollar 6 miles per dollar Premier Silver 5 miles per dollar 8 miles per dollar Premier Gold 6 miles per dollar 9 miles per dollar Premier Platinum 7 miles per dollar 10 miles per dollar Premier 1K 9 miles per dollar 12 miles per dollar These rates apply to base airfare and carrier-imposed surcharges and exclude taxes. Basic Economy and other base-option fares have different earning rules. This is mileage earned from flying, separate from whatever the card you use to buy the tickets earns. A general member earns twice as many flight miles with a qualifying card. A 1K doesn’t double their earning, but still picks up three more miles per eligible dollar. Spend $5,000 on eligible fares and that’s 15,000 additional miles at either status level. Then there’s the redemption side. United gives eligible primary cardholders: At least 10% off United and United Express award prices without Premier status. At least 15% off with Premier status. Access to additional Polaris business class Saver award inventory. More seats at the lower price can matter more than the percentage discount. At the minimum discounts, an award with a base price of 100,000 miles becomes 90,000 miles for a cardholder without status, or 85,000 for a cardholder with status. The discounts don’t cover partner-operated flights, Money + Miles bookings, or taxes and fees. You need to book through the primary cardholder’s MileagePlus account. Adding someone as an authorized user doesn’t give their MileagePlus account these benefits. The award pricing benefit can take up to five weeks after card issuance to become available. The No Annual Fee Card Has A $10,000 Spend Requirement To Unlock Benefits United GatewaySM Card‘s offer is 50,000 miles with just $1,000 in purchases and an added authorized user. That’s a record bonus and a low spending requirement. Chase is right to call it the card’s best offer ever. However, Gateway requires $10,000 in purchases in a calendar year to unlock the higher flight earning and cardmember award pricing. Once earned, the award pricing benefit lasts for the rest of that calendar year and the following one. I actually think that UnitedSM Explorer Card (which has a $0 annual fee the first year) and the UnitedSM Business Card are both better options. Which Offer Makes The Most Sense? UnitedSM Explorer Card is the base personal card. You get up to 80,000 miles and the better MileagePlus earning and award prices without a first year annual fee. It also comes with Group 2 boarding, two United Club one-time passes each year, and a free first checked bag for the primary cardholder and one companion on the same reservation. The bag benefit generally requires buying the tickets with the card. Club passes are subject to admission restrictions and capacity. The UnitedSM Business Card is especially attractive if you qualify. It matches the 100,000-mile maximum on the Club cards, adds 2,000 qualifying points, and costs $150 a year. It offers a $125 United travel credit after five United flight purchases of at least $100 each in a calendar year. And you get 5,000 anniversary miles when you also hold a personal Chase United card. United QuestSM Card has strong benefits if you’ll use them. The $350 annual fee buys $200 in United TravelBank cash after opening and at each anniversary, plus a 10,000-mile award flight discount starting at the first anniversary. It also provides 1,000 qualifying points annually starting the calendar year after opening. If the $200 credit replaces airfare you’d otherwise buy, you’re left evaluating $150 of the fee against the remaining benefits and that’s the annual fee of Explorer. The United ClubSM Card is for people who will use the lounges. It has a $695 annual fee and includes United Club membership. #6060. Yikes: FAA Union Claims Nationwide Ground Stop Was Totally Avoidable

On Friday, we saw a nationwide ground stop that lasted for around four hours, making it the longest ground stop that we’ve seen in the country in over 25 years, since 9/11. This is of course a major screw-up, and it’ll likely take some time before an investigation fully reveals what the root cause of this was.

So far, the response from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has been downright pitiful, and that’s the polite way of putting it. Along those lines, the union representing workers at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is suggesting that this might’ve been completely avoidable, because unlike in the past, no risk assessment was performed prior to the mistake that caused this mess.

On Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to update people on the state of the shutdown. The whole thing felt to me like an SNL skit, because Duffy and Mullin couldn’t even keep their narratives straight, and the whole message was so tone deaf.

Rather than thanking the public for their patience, Duffy went on a rant demanding $50 billion from Congress, suggesting it’s their fault that they haven’t given Trump money for the past year. On Friday night, Duffy suggested the following was the reason that our skies shut down:

“What happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down… I shouldn’t say they went down… they started to give us inconsistency with the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old air traffic control systems for the telecommunication issues behind the FAA nationwide ground stop on Friday."Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data," he said. "They started to give us inconsistency in the data… pic.twitter.com/5iX8mqL7RP

So he suggested that this was because of switches being overloaded due to how outdated the system is, which of course raised lots of questions about what made Friday different than any other day, in terms of the system being overloaded. Not surprisingly, he didn’t have a good answer, because he was just talking out of his you-know-what.

Very good set of questions from Luke Radel for Secretary Duffy and Secretary Mullin. pic.twitter.com/f6tlfDtbJG

Less than 24 hours later, Duffy switched his tune, explaining the situation as follows:

In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from old copper wire and they were bringing it over to fiber. That contractor that does the work for us is L3Harris. They are our legacy provider, they’ve been working for the FAA for over 20 years.”

“What we are working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said FAA contractor L3Harris was working at a remote location to switch telecommunication lines from cooper to fiber, which led to the longest nationwide shutdown of flights since the September 11, 2001, attacks https://t.co/6m0coVd6mo pic.twitter.com/5zdZoINAcA

So on Friday, the problem was that the switches got overloaded due to how old the system was, and Duffy used that to essentially make the press conference a $50 billion demand to modernize air traffic control (which I’m all in favor of, for the record, if done correctly, but this doesn’t seem to be the time or place for this). Then on Saturday, it was a mess up by a contractor.

Does anyone remember when press briefings during a period of crisis were about sharing facts, and not just making random stuff up, and sharing theories that suit narratives? Those were the days…

This is way beyond my area of expertise, but I’m sure I’m not alone in wondering how one contractor can make a mistake that just shuts down our entire aviation ecosystem? Shouldn’t there be a little more oversight so that such a major mistake can’t happen?”

This is where it gets interesting. PASS (“Professional Aviation Safety Specialists”) is the union representing 11,000 workers at the FAA. According to the union, historically projects like this would’ve been overseen by FAA employees with a risk assessment and more coordination, but that hasn’t been happening anymore. Here’s the statement:

The issue was isolated to two contractor owned and maintained routers that were being updated mid-day. Historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment. PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop yesterday.

PASS fully supports the administration’s efforts to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system. It must be recognized by the FAA that modernization will move more quickly with fewer disruptions if PASS is fully engaged.The employees represented by the union are on the front lines and they have the skills and expertise to make the Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) a reality. These employees should receive training on new equipment and could ensure more robust installation and optimization—if the workforce were properly staffed.

So a big question is when did FAA technicians stop being involved in these kinds of projects, in terms of coordination and risk assessment?

We don’t know to what extent this is related, but it of course has to be pointed out that in early 2025, Elon Musk’s DOGE (“Department of Government Efficiency”) laid off approximately 400 FAA employees. There wasn’t much transparency about who was laid off, though reports suggested that it included those tasked with aircraft safety inspections, and repairing air traffic control facilities.

One would hope that it will be investigated whether there’s any link here between the lack of oversight of projects like this, and the job cuts at the FAA.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has done an abhorrent job handling the nationwide air traffic control shutdown, in my opinion.

On Friday night, he took the time to come up with a random, convenient theory as to what happened, to suit his narrative. He demanded $50 billion from Congress (which Republicans have had control of for the past two years), and expressed no sympathy for the public that has been impacted by all of this. Then less than 24 hours later, he blamed contractors, saying they messed up some wire upgrades.

Understandably, we’re all wondering how the heck an upgrade to wiring in one place could shut down our entire air traffic system. The union representing FAA employees is suggesting that historically these projects would be overseen by FAA employees, and would also include a risk assessment, but they insist no FAA employees were involved here.

Duffy is right about one thing — there was definitely some incompetence here…

What do you make of these updates about the FAA ground stop?

anyone that thinks that what happened Friday was or is unique to the FAA or happens/happened just during this administration is living under a rock. The US government is the most incompetent organization for managing large capital projects and that is true from defense to IT to real estate. Friday just exposed how fragile the FAA's technology is but that has been the case for decades; every administration from both parties are responsible for how badly FAA technology has become. Yes, there was ZERO risk assessment - you don't do major technology upgrades in the middle of the afternoon on any day. L3Harris did not sufficiently test the conversion before it was made live - no different from CrowdStrike. This was just one of multiple major technology upgrades gone bad last week so it cuts across all of corporate America. yes, money needs to be spent to upgrade systems and conversion will be a piecemeal exercise because the system has to keep operating. The men and women that provide ATC services do an incredible job w/ what they are given - but they have an adversarial relationship w/ their employer just like every union. the real takeaway is how each airline is doing in returning to service to normal. DL and UA might get back to close to normal today. AA was already doing worse and tstorms are expected to hit N. Texas later today. WN was making progress before a bomb threat last night. B6 is their usual operational nightmare. Lower fuel prices are helping take the financial sting out of this meltdown but passengers are facing yet another operational meltdown that could have been managed better - both by the government and airlines.

Who in their right minds does a big upgrade mid-day Friday? The incompetence of this administration is beyond words.

There is definitely something rotten in Denmark. A lifetime ago I worked for a government agency. We would perform upgrades like these on Tuesday mornings at 2am, intentionally. That way if something happened the effect would be minor because traffic was low at that time. Additionally, if we had to call in extra workers Tuesday is the perfect day of the week for that. Friday afternoon is just a stupid time to do critical updates. If something goes wrong the effect is greater and try calling in extra workers on Friday afternoon. This doesn’t seem to have been coordinated properly. Besides how can one bad switch in one region cause a nationwide outage? That doesn’t make any sense.

This exposes just how dishonest Friday night's press conference was. Turns out gutting FAA oversight and letting a private vendor push an uncoordinated mid-day upgrade without a risk assessment ends badly—who knew?? The real fix isn't handing $50 billion to Duffy's cronies; it's staffing, training, and actually listening to the frontline FAA technicians who keep our skies safe.

#6059. Southwest Pilot Calls Out Nationwide Flight Shutdown As A Government Control Plot

A pilot, reportedly with Southwest Airlines, says he flew from Cancún to Phoenix without any communications problems. He’s concluded that Friday’s nationwide flight shutdown was a government operation to control people. He calls the whole thing “a big farce.” He managed to successfully complete his own flight, which was already in the air by the time trouble began, and claims that proves the whole thing was a scam. The video is from @mike4flight, the profile of Mike McHugh. Standing in a parking garage in uniform, he lists the facilities he spoke with and says they all worked fine. Then he offers his theory: So whatever’s going on, I think it’s designed to create fear and disruption and chaos, because that’s how the government gets control of things, controls people. Watch the pilot’s video He never explains how this advances the government’s goal, what additional control it gains, or why it wants that control. Which power are stranded passengers supposed to surrender? The government already decides whether planes can take off. Keeping people at the airport for hours accomplishes what, exactly? And how does costing airlines hundreds of millions of dollars in a day advance its goals? He says “I don’t know what’s going on,” but instead of then keeping quiet he decides to tell the world it’s a government operation. His fight went fine, but that doesn’t mean everything was actually fine. Some communications worked, others didn’t. Radar information could become unreliable even while a pilot could hear a controller. A pilot hears the frequencies he’s assigned at the times he’s using them. That doesn’t say much. The decision to let aircraft already airborne continue while stopping departures isn’t a contradiction. Limiting the number of flights controllers had to work given the conditions they faced made sense. Every landing reduced the workload. Every new departure would have added another aircraft needing instructions, separation and handoffs between controllers. Remaining capacity could be reserved for aircraft already flying. Working frequencies and contingency procedures could help bring those flights in without supporting a normal stream of new departures. The FAA’s ground stop rules cover facilities that are only partially unable to provide service. You don’t wait until every radio goes silent before reducing traffic. In fact, depending on when he flew, the ground stop may have helped make his trip uneventful. Fewer planes competing for the remaining capacity would make his experience easier. He may be pointing to the benefit of the restriction as evidence it wasn’t needed in the first place. Friday’s nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and was lifted around 8:15 p.m. It lasted over four hours. By early Saturday morning, there were more than 12,500 cancellations across Friday and Saturday. Looks like some stuck travelers got a concert from the singer of Hoobastank during the national air traffic shut down https://t.co/xWW5yE9JaP — Jennie Taer (@JennieSTaer) November 14, 2026 According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, legacy telecommunications switches and routers became overloaded, producing inconsistent radar information and communications at en route centers and airport approach facilities. He said the newer internet protocol switches hadn’t experienced these problems. The L3Harris-operated FAA telecommunications network carries voice and surveillance information between facilities. Trouble moving that information interrupts a controller’s radio audio and radar display. Apparently the break down came in Cisco 600-series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed to throw Duffy under the bus while trying to defend the administration. Standing beside him at the briefing, Mullin said the apparent problem involved Duffy and the FAA installing patches, equipment and technology that overwhelmed the older system. The new tech was “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy’s defense was that the new equipment hadn’t failed. Watch Markwayne Mullin explain the apparent cause beside Sean Duffy When I reviewed the administration’s modernization plan, I warned that compressing decades of hardware replacements, software integrations and transitions into 36 months brought risks of service disruption. Duffy used the briefing to press Congress for $50 billion. He wants more taxpayer money rather than user fees to prop up an agency that’s failed to modernize with the billions given to it before, without explaining why only money – and not fixing project management, budgeting and leadership at the agency – is all that’s needed. He calls the whole thing “a big farce.” He managed to successfully complete his own flight, which was already in the air by the time trouble began, and claims that proves the whole thing was a scam.

The video is from @mike4flight, the profile of Mike McHugh. Standing in a parking garage in uniform, he lists the facilities he spoke with and says they all worked fine. Then he offers his theory:

So whatever’s going on, I think it’s designed to create fear and disruption and chaos, because that’s how the government gets control of things, controls people.

And how does costing airlines hundreds of millions of dollars in a day advance its goals?

He says “I don’t know what’s going on,” but instead of then keeping quiet he decides to tell the world it’s a government operation.

His fight went fine, but that doesn’t mean everything was actually fine. Some communications worked, others didn’t. Radar information could become unreliable even while a pilot could hear a controller. A pilot hears the frequencies he’s assigned at the times he’s using them. That doesn’t say much. Friday’s nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and was lifted around 8:15 p.m. It lasted over four hours. By early Saturday morning, there were more than 12,500 cancellations across Friday and Saturday.

Looks like some stuck travelers got a concert from the singer of Hoobastank during the national air traffic shut down https://t.co/xWW5yE9JaP

— Jennie Taer (@JennieSTaer) November 14, 2026

According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, legacy telecommunications switches and routers became overloaded, producing inconsistent radar information and communications at en route centers and airport approach facilities. He said the newer internet protocol switches hadn’t experienced these problems.

The L3Harris-operated FAA telecommunications network carries voice and surveillance information between facilities. Trouble moving that information interrupts a controller’s radio audio and radar display. Apparently the break down came in Cisco 600-series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed to throw Duffy under the bus while trying to defend the administration. Standing beside him at the briefing, Mullin said the apparent problem involved Duffy and the FAA installing patches, equipment and technology that overwhelmed the older system. The new tech was “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy’s defense was that the new equipment hadn’t failed.

Watch Markwayne Mullin explain the apparent cause beside Sean Duffy

When I reviewed the administration’s modernization plan, I warned that compressing decades of hardware replacements, software integrations and transitions into 36 months brought risks of service disruption.

Duffy used the briefing to press Congress for $50 billion. He wants more taxpayer money rather than user fees to prop up an agency that’s failed to modernize with the billions given to it before, without explaining why only money – and not fixing project management, budgeting and leadership at the agency – is all that’s needed.

I wouldn’t want this nut case to be the pilot on any flight I happen to be on.

Southwest has way more than their fair share of nut jobs. Case and point.

Airlines pay for FAA “services” by the airport fees and fees (taxes) placed on passenger tickets. General Aviation pays for FAA services with a high “fuel tax”. All of this money goes into the “kitty” for use by the FAA. BUT…Congress (both parties!!) will steal this money for pet projects…kinda like the “bridge to nowhere” in Alaska. The FAA doesn’t/won’t take any advice from the NTSB to fix issues related to aviation safety. The DCA regional jet/Army helicopter crash is a PRIME example of complete incompetence. The NTSB says, “get your communications fixed”, “don’t let helicopters fly in KDCA airspace”. Does the Congress or FAA comply? HELL NO! There are those that proffer “privatizing” the FAA. EVEN WORSE! Canada’s private “FAA” NAV CANADA charges for EVERYTHING. A student wants to shoot “touch & go’s”…there’s a charge to your credit card or FBO. You want to shoot several instrument approaches…same thing. You want to fly cross country…a charge. That’s why Canadian student pilots come to the US for training. While the hourly rate may be higher in USD, it’s offset by not being nickel & dimed to death. If you want to point a finger, point it at both senators and your congressman. THEY are the problem!

Did anyone watch the 1997 movie Conspiracy Theory? Crazy conspiracy theories are nuts, unless they are true. Of course, I think the Southwest Pilot is unlikely in the extreme. However, his theory is more likely than my theory that I am going to win $1 billion in the lottery. Just saying.

More serious comment. Cisco routers from 2001 to 2006. I think that is Window XP level technology. Since then, Microsoft forced me to buy a Windows 7 computer. Then a Windows 10 computer. I am being forces to shop for a Window 11 computer. No wonder the update didn’t work.

As an IT professional for several decades (financial institutions, oil&gas businesses and supply chain management for the world’s largest food company), I have never known critical systems to be patched or updated during normal business hours. That just never happens. Don’t know what really happened yesterday nor with the Microsoft outage but the stories that are being told that it was updates gone bad, are lies.

There is an element of truth. Project 2025 has a section that discusses dismantling the FAA and privatizing the system. And in general, yes, fascist regimes do sow chaos and distrust in existing systems as a form of control over the population.

Back in 1984 Charles Perrow wrote a book called, “Normal Accidents”. His contention is that as systems get more complicated thy are more likely to have points where failures magnify through the tightly coupling of various parts. Eventually these can cascade into a catastrophic collapse of the entire system. These situations may be reduced, and to some extent mitigated with good designs and training, but by the very nature of complexity will still occur in totally unexpected ways. In fact, building in redundancies can sometimes be counter-productive as it makes systems even more complicated and prone to failure.

We may have reached this point in air traffic control, made worse by old equipment and a sluggish bureaucracy that reacts rather than is proactive in avoiding accidents. You don’t need a vast plot (though I admit that I wondered if this was the start of a coup) to have a total system failure. One thing does seem likely, and that is more such events will occur, and without intelligent action they will be more frequent.

I remember being on 42nd street Times Square and seeing the street filled with people trying to get home. I was going to walk home to my apartment on the West Side, then my ex-girlfriend called me and said “Are you going to leave me alone during the black out”, so I stayed with her. (3) Regarding LS’s comment. MMMMMaaaaaayyyyyyyBBeeee. Yea, Alex Jones’s InfoWars used to believe that the Obama administration was going to do a military coop too. (4) Remembering all the drones that were flying all over the USA during the previous administration. Nobody ever really told us why that happened. With the Nationwide Shutdown, I personally do not think they are telling us what actually happened. My bet is on a hack of some sort. Not sure we will ever find out. WTH. I don’t think the government still has not released all the 1963 Kennedy assassination information yet.

#6058. World Of Hyatt Credit Card Review: Why It’s My Go-To Hotel Card

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is Hyatt’s co-branded Chase personal credit card. The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers strong benefits that can easily offset that, including an anniversary free night award, elite nights toward status, and more. It can even be worth spending money on the card, in order to unlock an additional free night and/or elite status.

This post is my in-depth World of Hyatt Card review. What makes Hyatt’s personal credit card so brilliant is that it’s worth having regardless of whether you want to keep it just for the ongoing perks, or whether you want to spend money on it.

Before I get into my World of Hyatt Credit Card review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:

Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the World of Hyatt Credit Card:

When we apply for credit cards, some of the most important factors are the welcome bonus, the eligibility rules for getting the card, and the annual fee. How does the World of Hyatt Credit Card do on those fronts? Let’s take a look.

At the moment, the World of Hyatt Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you can earn four free night awards after spending $5,000 within the first three months. Each free night award is valid at a Category 1-4 World of Hyatt property.

World of Hyatt Category 4 properties retail for up to 25,000 points per night, so the absolute maximum value of this offer is 100,000 points. However, I of course wouldn’t value it that highly. That’s because these free night awards expire 12 months after they’re issued, and you also can’t top off these awards to redeem at more expensive properties. So actually maxing out the value of these isn’t easy.

One thing I should mention is that while I don’t love the lack of flexibility of this welcome offer, it’s significantly better than the standard bonus, which tends to be lackluster. Obviously Chase and Hyatt know that this is a card people will get for the long term value, rather than just for the bonus.

For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each.

When you pull up the World of Hyatt Credit Card application, you’ll see the following terms:

This product is available to you if you do not have this card and have not received a new cardmember bonus for this card in the past 24 months.

This is good news, as eligibility is considered independently of any other Chase credit card, and it’s also considered independently of the World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more).

It’s also worth remembering the Chase 5/24 rule, whereby you sometimes won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (certain business cards are excluded). However, that no longer seems to be consistently enforced.

Fortunately nowadays Chase uses a pop-up feature during the application process, which should let you know if you’re not eligible for the bonus on a card (this appears after submitting your application), before there’s a hard pull on your credit.

There’s not a consistent rule as to what credit score you need to be approved for the World of Hyatt Credit Card. In general, I’d recommend having a credit score in the “good” to “excellent” range.

Personally, I’d hope to have a credit score of at least 700. That being said, people with scores lower than that have been approved, and conversely, people with scores higher than that have been rejected. There are lots of factors that go into approval. Chase will consider your income, your credit history, how much credit Chase has already extended you, etc.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee. You can add additional cardmembers to your account at no extra cost. This annual fee is well worth it even if you don’t spend money on the card, since you get an anniversary free night award that can be redeemed at hotels costing $250+ per night.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s an excellent card for purchases abroad. That’s especially true when staying with Hyatt abroad, as well as for dining and commuting outside the US.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers pretty good points earning opportunities. While this isn’t the card that I use for all of my spending, I strategically spend money on the card, and it works great for me. How good are the points earning rates? Here are the very basics, and then I’ll discuss it in more detail below:

Let me emphasize that points earning is only part of the value proposition of spending on the card. It’s also about being able to earn elite status, which I’ll cover in more detail a bit later.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 4x points for spending at Hyatt hotels and resorts, including Mr & Mrs Smith properties. That’s a solid return on hotel spending, though admittedly it doesn’t beat the return you get on the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more), which also offers 4x points on hotel purchases, and points can be moved to World of Hyatt.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 5.6% return on Hyatt spending.

Keep in mind that this is all in addition to the standard points earning at properties. World of Hyatt members ordinarily earn 5x points per dollar spent, plus elite bonuses of 10-30%. So the 4x points stacks on top of that.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points for restaurant spending globally. That’s obviously a widely useful return, though in fairness, it’s also hard to get too excited about 2x points in this category, given the number of cards that offer 3-5x points on dining spending.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on restaurant spending.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points on airline tickets purchased globally directly from airlines. While it’s nice to have this as a bonus category, again, it’s hard to get too excited about 2x points, given the number of cards that offer 3-5x points on airfare spending.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on airfare spending.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points on fitness clubs and gym memberships. For anyone wondering, this also includes group fitness businesses, like Barry’s Bootcamp, SoulCycle, etc. It’s nice to have this as a bonus category, since it’s pretty rare to see a bonus for these kinds of purchases. However, with other cards offering 2x points on everyday spending, it’s not all that exciting.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on fitness spending.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points on local transit and commuting, which includes ride share services such as Lyft and Uber.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on local transit and commuting spending.

The World of Hyatt Card offers 1x points per dollar spent on everyday spending. Generally speaking, there are better cards for everyday spending, though as I’ll explain below, some of the spending bonuses could make it worth shifting spending onto this card.

The area where the World of Hyatt Credit Card really excels is when it comes to the benefits it offers. In my opinion, these benefits more than justify the annual fee, regardless of whether you’re spending nothing on the card, or are spending a significant amount. Specifically, the benefits largely center around earning free nights award and elite status, so let’s cover those details.

Just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a Category 1-4 free night award on your account anniversary every year. This will be issued shortly after your anniversary and is valid for 12 months.

Categories 1-4 cover a majority of Hyatt’s properties, and those hotels can retail for up to 25,000 points per night. I’ve consistently been able to redeem these at hotels costing $250+ per night, so that (way) more than justifies the annual fee.

One downside worth flagging is that you unfortunately can’t top off these awards with additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. That’s quite the contrast to the free night awards issued by IHG One Rewards and Marriott Bonvoy.

Beyond the anniversary free night award just for being a cardmember, the World of Hyatt Card offers a second free night award if you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year. This could be a major incentive to spend money on the card, as it makes $15,000 in spending quite a good sweet spot.

You receive World of Hyatt’s entry-level Discoverist status for as long as you have the World of Hyatt Card. The status will post for the primary cardmember shortly after you are approved. Perks of Discoverist status include the following:

Don’t get too excited here, but some status is better than no status! Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite nights or 25,000 base points (which correlates to $5,000 in spending).

The World of Hyatt Card gives you five elite qualifying nights toward status annually just for being a cardmember. You will receive these within eight weeks of being approved for the card (though usually much faster), and in subsequent years they will post within eight weeks of January 1.

This will be useful if you’re hoping to earn World of Hyatt Explorist status, World of Hyatt Globalist status, and/or World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards. For context, World of Hyatt Explorist status requires 30 elite nights, while World of Hyatt Globalist status requires 60 elite nights.

In addition to the five elite nights you get just for having the World of Hyatt Card, you earn a further two elite qualifying nights for every $5,000 you spend on the card. This means that in theory, you could spend your way all the way to Explorist or Globalist status, if you wanted to.

Reaching the $5,000 threshold has nothing to do with the calendar or cardmember year — the counter simply resets every time you spend $5,000, and then you start earning toward your next two elite nights. So if you spend $4,000 in one year and $1,000 in the next year, you’d get two elite nights in the second year.

The World of Hyatt Card offers auto rental collision damage waiver coverage. Decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card. Coverage is provided for theft and collision damage for most cars in the United States and abroad. Do note that in the US, the coverage is secondary to your personal insurance, though.

The World of Hyatt Card offers a variety of protection when traveling, including the following:

I’d consider World of Hyatt points to be among the most valuable hotel points currencies out there, though admittedly they’ve been devalued a bit over time.

The best value for redeeming World of Hyatt points is using the free night award chart. The great thing is that you earn elite nights for your stay even if you’re redeeming points or using a free night award. Below is World of Hyatt’s award chart.

There’s value to be had at all levels of the chart. As a general rule of thumb, I try to redeem at properties where I’m getting more than two cents of value per point. That’s because personally I value World of Hyatt points at ~1.4 cents each. It’s also worth being aware of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa Awards, which let you redeem points toward on-property spending.

Let me answer this very simply. If you’re eligible for the World of Hyatt Credit Card and have any interest in staying at Hyatt properties then yes, the World of Hyatt Credit Card is absolutely worth it. This is a card I personally have, and that I wholeheartedly recommend.

As I see it, the World of Hyatt Card is good for:

Meanwhile the World of Hyatt Card is probably not good for:

Personally, my approach is to put $15,000 of spending on the World of Hyatt Card every calendar year, and I think that’s a real sweet spot. By spending $15,000 on the card in a year you receive:

Even taking the value of the elite nights out of the equation, if you spend $15,000 on the card in categories on which you otherwise wouldn’t earn bonus points, you’re earning a Category 1-4 certificate that could be redeemed at a hotel potentially costing up to 25,000 points. That’s potentially like earning over two World of Hyatt points per dollar spent, which is a great return on everyday spending.

The World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more) could be a good option for any small business looking to earn Hyatt points or status. Here’s how the two cards compare:

Personally I think the personal card is generally more rewarding, though the business version of the card earns you elite nights at an accelerated rate. See my comparison of the two cards.

World of Hyatt Globalist status requires 60 elite nights per year, so how does the math work on spending your way to Globalist status with the World of Hyatt Credit Card? If you were to earn Globalist status from scratch exclusively with this credit card, you’d need to spend $140,000:

Personally I’d never spend all the way to Globalist status, but rather I’d use a hybrid approach, and would earn Globalist status partly through credit card spending and partly through actual stays. After all, if you’re not actually staying a significant number of nights, what’s the point of earning the status?

It’s also worth emphasizing that if your goal is to just spend your way toward elite status, the World of Hyatt Business Card would be the best option, since you’d earn the status after $120,000 in spending (with no head start).

Globalist status is my favorite top-tier hotel status, and it comes with all kinds of awesome perks. Many of the benefits are tied to the Milestone Rewards program, but just to give you a sense of what you could receive if you earned 60 elite nights in a calendar year:

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is an exceptional hotel credit card. It’s a card I have, and a card I spend at least $15,000 on per year.

The card is worth having even if you don’t plan on putting spending on it — you get an anniversary free night award you can use at a hotel that costs significantly more than the annual fee, you get complimentary Discoverist status, and you get five elite nights toward a higher status tier.

Beyond that, it can be worth putting spending on the card, thanks to the unique bonus categories (4x points on Hyatt stays and 2x points on fitness and gyms), as well as the additional elite nights and second free night award.
